content: Fucales is an order within the phylum Phaeophyta, commonly known as brown algae. Organisms belonging to this order are referred to as fucoids. Detailed taxonomic information about the families within Fucales, as well as other algae, can be accessed through the AlgaeBase database. The class Phaeophyceae, to which Fucales belongs, is part of the division Heterokontophyta. The name Phaeophyceae is derived from the Greek words phaios, meaning brown, and phyton, meaning plant. Members of this class include some of the largest marine plants, although some species are small and delicate in structure. The class Phaeophyceae is divided into several orders, as outlined by Hoek in 1995. These orders include Ectocarpales, Sphacelariales, Syringodermatales, Dictyotales, Scytosiphonales, Cutleriales, Dictyosiphonales, Chordariales, Sporochnales, Desmarestiales, Laminariales, Fucales, Durvillaeales, and Ascoseirales. Among these, the order Fucales includes many common littoral seaweeds. Members of Fucales exhibit a typical seaweed morphology, consisting of a holdfast, a stipe, and a lamina. The lamina is often highly branched and may contain gas-filled bladders that aid in buoyancy. Growth in these organisms occurs through the division of apical cells. Fucales are oogamous, meaning their reproduction involves the fusion of a small, motile male gamete with a larger, non-motile female gamete. As their name suggests, their pigmentation is predominantly brown due to the presence of specific pigments. All species within this order are multicellular. The detailed characteristics of Fucales are complex and include specific features such as the structure of their flagella, the shape of their chloroplasts, the composition of their cell walls, and the intricacies of their life cycle. Globally, there are approximately 1,500 to 2,000 species of brown seaweeds, including those within the order Fucales.
